post1.text:
Hiring more executives is not a scaling strategy. It is a delay tactic.

When companies hit $50M and start pushing toward $500M, the instinct is to stack the leadership bench. Bring in senior talent, distribute the load, buy yourself breathing room. But the data tells a different story. Companies that scale successfully do not just add leaders. They change how leadership itself works.

Three things separating the companies that make it from the ones that plateau:

1. Leaders at scale make fewer decisions, not more. They build systems that decide for them.

2. The CEO's job transforms completely between $50M and $200M. Those who do not redefine their role become the ceiling.

3. Culture is not an HR initiative at this stage. It is a operating lever that either accelerates growth or quietly kills it.

Alpha Compute's recent executive team expansion illustrates this well. The move was not just about headcount. It was a deliberate restructuring of how leadership would function across a global operation.

What does your leadership model actually need to look like two years from now?

#Leadership #ScalingBusiness #ExecutiveGrowth

post2.text:
A recent piece in HousingWire caught our attention. Buffini and Company just added three senior executives specifically to scale their coaching business.

On the surface, that looks like a straightforward hiring story. But for any company in the $50M to $500M range, there is a more important question underneath it: Are you adding leaders to handle today's volume, or to build the structure that handles tomorrow's?

There is a real difference. One is reactive. The other is a growth architecture decision.

At Autobahn, we work with leadership teams navigating exactly this inflection point. The companies that scale well are the ones that hire for the org chart they need 18 months from now, not the one they have today.

Read the full article here and think about where your next leadership hire is actually aimed: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMicEFVX3lxTE80SmJLNXdFS1VDcE9QNXQ2YzNFUDNUSzItcWljNWEyb2NEUVJ0UzdweEIzaVZyclAyWk5fcW54Nlo2U21GSVVoMHFJaVpLSFdaMU1tMXRIWU8wMTJvc3RJNTM5VkhoaVFxZnZFM0VlWVU

post3.text:
Every scaling company eventually hits the same wall. The leadership style that got you to $50M starts working against you on the way to $500M.

Chapter 1 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, is called Lead Like Lives Depend On It. Written by Katherine Slain, it confronts something most leadership books avoid: the moment a founder or executive has to fundamentally change who they are as a leader, not just what they do.

Cyrille Bessière's well-documented track record of scaling companies reflects this exact principle. The executives who scale well are not the ones with the best instincts. They are the ones who build leadership capacity that outlasts their own involvement in every decision.

Katherine's chapter gives you a framework for getting there before the growing pains force your hand.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Most companies approaching $500M are not being held back by their market, their product, or their competition. They are being held back by a leadership model built for a company half their size. The executives who figure this out early do not just grow faster. They build organizations that do not need them to be everywhere at once. Here is what that shift actually looks like.

articles.snippet: Many entrepreneurs are ready to pass the torch, but few are prepared.  BDC.ca

post1.text:
Most business owners think about their exit too late. By the time they're ready to sell, the window to maximize their multiple has already closed.

Here's what actually drives valuation at the $50M+ level, and it's not what most owners focus on.

Silicon Valley Bank's research on exit timing makes something clear: market conditions matter far less than internal readiness. Buyers pay premiums for businesses that don't need their owner to function.

Three things that move the needle before you go to market:

1. Revenue concentration risk. If your top three clients represent more than 40% of revenue, sophisticated buyers will discount you immediately.

2. Management bench depth. A leadership team that can operate independently post-close is worth real money at the negotiating table.

3. Clean, auditable financials. Deals die in due diligence. Sellers who can produce three years of clean statements compress timelines and protect their number.

The companies that extract the most value from a sale are the ones that prepared as if they were never going to sell.

What are you doing today that would hold up under buyer scrutiny?

post2.text:
A recent piece from J.P. Morgan Private Bank walks through the core business exit strategies available to owners, from strategic sales to private equity recaps to family succession.

It's a solid overview. But here's what it doesn't address: for companies in the $50M to $500M range, the strategy you choose has to match where your business actually is, not where you hope it is.

Too many scaling companies pursue a premium exit before they've built the infrastructure to support one. The result is a lower multiple, a longer process, or a deal that falls apart entirely.

If you're in that growth corridor, the time to decide how you exit is at least three years before you plan to. That's when the real value creation happens.

Morgan piece here and reach out if you want to pressure-test your current position: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMitwFBVV95cUxOalJUT0c3NEFPTndZX08zeGN0dXVFOEJVcmVLRml0QUNjb2xXU3Nxd2ZjOW1mUVUtc0F6SDZ0M056b2Rpd21ZZWF6aVBpOHZESjRiMEtKYk13Sm52VTJJTzV5ZzhFVTE5LVVtcVN4aVpiUzJYUUEtclFONlM4S0NzS3owaFRDT3p6Z2NoZlhjSUh1QnhsWTkyT3pKQkJZR3YxWnZHSHpHTDQ3MEtSRDdBb1JDTVJrb1U

post3.text:
BDC recently reported that while many entrepreneurs are emotionally ready to exit, very few have done the operational work to actually pull it off on their terms.

That gap, between readiness to leave and readiness to sell well, is exactly what Chapter 2 of our upcoming book tackles head on.

In 'Maximize Your Multiple to Achieve Your Exit,' authors Paul Belair and George Hohman lay out what buyers are actually underwriting when they look at a $50M to $500M business. Hint: it goes well beyond your EBITDA number.

One thing they make clear early: the levers that increase your multiple are not the same levers that grew your revenue. Scaling and exiting require entirely different thinking, and most owners conflate the two until it costs them.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Most business owners spend decades building their company and weeks preparing to sell it. That imbalance is expensive. For companies between $50M and $500M, the difference between a good exit and a great one is rarely timing or market conditions. It's the internal work that happens two to four years before a buyer ever sees your financials. Here's what that work actually looks like.

post1.text:
Most strategic plans fail not because the strategy is wrong, but because execution is treated as an afterthought.

Forbes recently explored why leadership teams consistently fall short on strategy execution. The findings point to a pattern we see constantly at Autobahn: companies at the $50M mark confuse having a plan with having a process.

Three things scaling companies get wrong:

1. Strategy lives in a deck, not in daily decisions. If your frontline managers cannot connect their weekly priorities to your three-year goals, your plan is a document, not a system.

2. Accountability is assumed, not designed. Without clear owners and cadences, execution defaults to whoever is loudest in the room.

3. Leaders review strategy once a year, then wonder why nothing changed. Execution requires a rhythm, not a retreat.

Companies that scale past $100M treat their operating cadence as a competitive advantage, not an administrative task.

So here is the real question: does your team know what winning looks like this quarter, or just this year?

post2.text:
A recent piece in SmartBrief laid out a practical framework for building a plan-execution process that actually delivers results. It is worth a read for any leadership team that has watched a solid strategy stall the moment it left the conference room.

Here is what we would add for companies scaling from $50M and beyond: the gap between planning and execution widens fast as your organization grows. What worked when your senior team could course-correct in a hallway conversation breaks down completely when you have multiple divisions, geographies, or product lines in motion.

At that stage, execution is not a soft skill. It is an infrastructure problem that requires deliberate design.

If your strategy execution feels inconsistent right now, start by asking whether your process is built for the company you are today or the one you were three years ago.

Read the full article here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMimAFBVV95cUxNRk8xX0ZPak91anhUdC1rSXY5X2FVMnBhb1J6bUFsT2VVdU5KbXhFNDRRaEdvMkk5M0EwVU5qajdsRHFlOVlINWZDckE3UU1pQ2xHdGFuTzBiSm9BNURLMDV3NnJHWU1zNlRQa1Q3MlREVFFPd2VCUWJtTWk0VTZfRTJDd09WenJMQ0hiQzJlNXpab1VNSVdkbQ?oc=5

post3.text:
Strategic planning gets a lot of attention. Execution gets a lot of excuses.

In Chapter 3 of Rock Your Business, 'What We Learned Selling Fish Food and Nike Shoes,' authors Rafa Loyo and Jim Randall share what two very different industries taught them about why execution breaks down at scale and what leaders actually have to change to fix it.

The insight that will stick with you: the strategy you can execute with discipline will always outperform the perfect strategy you cannot. Loyo and Randall show how companies moving through the $50M to $500M corridor often carry planning habits that worked early on but quietly become the ceiling that stops further growth.

This chapter will challenge how you think about the relationship between your leadership team and your operating rhythm.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Most leadership teams do not have a strategy problem. They have an execution infrastructure problem. The plan looks solid in the room and falls apart in the field. For companies scaling past $50M, closing that gap is not about working harder or holding more meetings. It is about redesigning how decisions, accountability, and priorities actually flow through a growing organization.

post1.text:
Most $50M+ companies don't have a sales strategy. They have a sales habit.

There's a difference. A habit is what your team does because it worked three years ago. A strategy is a deliberate system built around how your best customers actually buy today.

Recent research from McKinsey confirms this gap is widening. B2B companies that treat growth as a revenue architecture problem are pulling away from those that treat it as a headcount problem. The threshold for survival is rising, and instinct-driven selling is no longer enough.

Here's what that means practically:

1. If you can't describe your ideal customer's buying journey in writing, you don't have a strategy.
2. Sales and marketing alignment isn't a cultural goal. It's a revenue lever.
3. The companies scaling past $100M have documented repeatable motions. Not heroic reps.

You can't optimize what you haven't defined.

So be honest: does your team have a sales strategy, or just a quota?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Bain and Company breaks down what separates B2B growth winners from companies stuck in neutral. The short version: winners invest in commercial capabilities before they feel the pressure to, not after.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern constantly with scaling companies. Leadership waits until revenue plateaus to audit the sales function. By then, six to twelve months of momentum are already gone.

For companies between $50M and $200M, the window to build a real sales engine is now. Not when growth slows. Not after the next hire. Now.

If you are curious what those differentiating commercial investments actually look like, the Bain piece is worth your time.

That chapter, written by Deb and Brandon, makes an uncomfortable case that most scaling companies are funding their competitors' growth through their own sales inaction. post1.text:
Your brand is not your logo. It is not your tagline. It is the feeling people get when they interact with your company, and most $50M+ businesses have no idea what that feeling actually is.

Ulta Beauty's CMO recently made this clear: brand building and customer experience are not separate functions. They are the same function. Companies that treat them as separate are leaving serious revenue on the table.

Here is what scaling companies get wrong about marketing:

1. They invest in visibility before they have established identity. Reach without clarity just spreads confusion faster.

2. They measure marketing by leads generated, not by trust built. Trust is what actually drives repeat revenue at scale.

3. They let their brand drift as they grow. What got you to $50M is rarely what will carry you to $500M. Your brand needs active management, not just active spend.

If your best customers tried to describe your company to a stranger today, would their answers match?

#Branding #BusinessGrowth #ScalingUp

post2.text:
A recent piece in Adweek took a close look at how Campari keeps heritage brands culturally relevant across decades and markets. The throughline was striking: they treat brand identity as a living system, not a fixed asset.

For companies scaling from $50M toward $500M, this matters more than most leaders realize. At that stage, your brand is being stretched across new markets, new hires, and new customer expectations all at once. Without intentional stewardship, it quietly loses its shape.

The companies that scale well do not just protect their brand. They actively evolve it while keeping its core intact. That is a discipline, not an accident.

If your brand strategy has not been pressure-tested against your growth plan lately, that is worth fixing now.

Ulta Beauty's approach to blending brand identity with customer experience is exactly the kind of thinking Chapter 5 of our upcoming book tackles head-on.

The chapter is called "What Does Your Marketing Smell Like?" and it was written by Kayli Simpson and Yasmin West. The title is intentional. Your marketing leaves an impression whether you have designed that impression or not. Most scaling companies discover this the hard way.

Kayli and Yasmin lay out a framework for understanding what your brand is actually communicating at every touchpoint, not just the ones you are paying attention to. One insight that will stick with you: the gap between what you think your brand says and what your customers actually experience is often where growth stalls.

post1.text:
Hiring more people faster is not a growth strategy. It is a liability strategy.

Most companies scaling past $50M treat talent acquisition like a volume game. Post more roles, fill more seats, repeat. But SHRM's latest research on 2026 hiring trends makes something clear: the companies winning on talent are the ones hiring with precision, not speed.

Here is what that looks like in practice for scaling businesses:

1. Define the role's output before you define the candidate. Hiring around job descriptions is backwards. Hire around measurable results.

2. Your first 10 hires in a new function set the culture of that function permanently. Mistakes compound fast at scale.

3. A bad hire at the $100M stage does not cost you a salary. It costs you market position, team trust, and six to eighteen months of recovery time.

Growth companies do not have the margin to treat hiring as a numbers game. The leaders who understand that are the ones building organizations that actually survive scale.

What does your current hiring process optimize for: speed, or fit?

post2.text:
A recent piece in UC Today raised a point that every scaling company needs to hear: your HR technology platform may not be solving your talent problems. It may be making them permanent.

The argument is straightforward. If your hiring process is broken, automating it at scale does not fix it. It just reproduces the same bad decisions faster and across more of your business.

At Autobahn, we see this constantly with companies moving through the $50M to $200M range. Leaders invest in better tools before they have built better processes. The tool becomes the excuse not to fix the underlying problem.

Technology should accelerate a sound talent strategy. It cannot replace one.

If your team is about to invest in a new HCM or ATS platform, read this first: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiqgFBVV95cUxQWjRQeU5RQWw1SlRfNElDUmhDVDFNUDBXeTE1NlJUOVI2TmVTVGY0aVpTVDJXYlh2bm1PWXhFUkFVZFZQT2tfWDQxMFowcm5jWWRLWlpPNFp5bUJyMXlhdnR5NkxXWTBVWGFzTDVDaGVNYnZEVjRxSEVSQW9jVmZzbGVyTjYwSzZBUTd0LWtvWWlyOEk5Qmg5bEduaHRuVTNTdUhqVDhETGFtZw?oc=5

post3.text:
SHRM is reporting that the rules of hiring are fundamentally shifting toward precision over volume. We have been saying this to our clients for years, and it is a core reason Chapter 6 of our upcoming book addresses it head on.

Chapter 6, The Talent Engine, written by Caleb Hawkins, Darla Klein, and Yasmin West, goes beyond the usual advice about culture and retention. One of the insights that stops leaders cold: most scaling companies do not have a hiring problem. They have a clarity problem. They cannot articulate what a great hire actually produces in the first 90 days, so they default to credentials and gut instinct.

That gap becomes very expensive between $50M and $500M.

The chapter gives leaders a framework for building a talent engine that scales with the business, not against it.

post1.text:
More KPIs do not make better leaders. They make busier ones.

Most companies scaling past $50M fall into the same trap: they add metrics every quarter and call it accountability. What they actually create is noise. When everyone is watching everything, no one is responsible for anything.

Hootsuite recently published a roundup of 31 social media metrics worth tracking. Thirty-one. That list is useful for a marketing team. It is a liability for an executive team trying to steer a company.

Here is what high-performing leadership teams at this growth stage actually do differently:

They limit their core scorecard to 5 to 7 metrics that directly connect to revenue, retention, or operational health. They assign a single owner to each number. No owner, no metric. They review trends, not just snapshots, because a number without direction tells you nothing.

The companies that scale fastest are not the ones tracking the most. They are the ones who act fastest on the least amount of meaningful data.

How many KPIs on your current scorecard has no one looked at in the last 30 days?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Business.com walked through 14 tools companies can use to track KPIs. Solid list, practical options, worth a look if you are evaluating your current stack.

But here is what the article does not address: the tool is never the problem.

Companies scaling from $50M toward $500M rarely struggle because they lack software. They struggle because they have not agreed on which numbers actually matter and who owns them. You can plug the best dashboard in the world into a team without that clarity and get very expensive confusion.

Before you evaluate any new tool, answer two questions first. What decisions does this data need to drive? And who loses sleep if that number moves in the wrong direction?

Get those answers right, then pick your tool.

https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMingFBVV95cUxQcWNPSTVTUDVYYURoVkZKa0ItNEtQbmJqWlNJTlIzUVZqclAxMHFaajNobC1JbGNkZGZVajN6MWJLT1pJcXktVG10VG8zUUljdU43NU5WR1cyNDB4QkxONlJkb3hJR2FfNzdGZHd1VWhPbTktdU1vdTEzamFWY2ZFVDNKUFIwRG91ZDdWU1UyN2twNFpLd1JjU3EzTUpjdw?oc=5

post3.text:
Oracle NetSuite recently published a breakdown of 11 KPIs every hospitality business should track. It is a useful industry-specific guide. And it points to a challenge that shows up in every sector at every growth stage: knowing which metrics to watch and knowing what to do when they move are two completely different skills.

Chapter 7 of Rock Your Business tackles this head-on. Titled Death by KPIs, the chapter was written by Hector Arias, Matt Radicelli, and Jim Randall. They work with leadership teams that are drowning in data and starving for direction. Their core argument is that most scorecards are built to report what happened, not to drive what happens next.

The shift they describe is specific, and it changes how executive teams run their weekly meetings.

Rock Your Business, by Jonathan Slain and Katherine Slain, available soon. Follow us for updates.

articles.snippet: C.E.O.s Say the A.I. Rollout Is Going Well. Employees Feel Differently.  The New York Times

post1.text:
AI is not a productivity problem. It is a perception problem.

A global study from TCS found that 84% of executives cite productivity as AI's top benefit. Yet when you look closer at the data coming out of boardrooms versus break rooms, there is a serious disconnect between what leaders believe is happening and what employees are actually experiencing on the ground.

For leaders scaling companies past $50M, that gap is not a morale issue. It is a strategic risk.

Three things worth internalizing right now:

1. Adoption without integration is just expensive experimentation. AI tools sitting alongside broken workflows do not compound returns.

2. ROI from AI rarely shows up where you deployed it. The gains often appear two or three functions away from the original investment.

3. Your managers are the multiplier. If they are skeptical or uninformed, your AI rollout flatlines regardless of the technology.

Executive confidence in AI is not the same as organizational readiness for AI.

So here is the real question: Are you measuring what your AI tools are actually changing, or just what you hope they are changing?

post2.text:
A recent piece in The New York Times surfaced something that should stop every growth-stage CEO mid-scroll: executives believe their AI rollouts are going well. Employees largely disagree.

That is not a communication problem. That is a scaling problem.

At Autobahn Consultants, we work with companies navigating the $50M to $500M corridor, and this disconnect shows up constantly. Leaders invest in AI, announce the initiative, and assume adoption follows. It rarely does without deliberate infrastructure around it.

The companies that actually capture AI's upside are building it into how decisions get made, not just how tasks get done.

If your team and your leadership are telling two different stories about how AI is working inside your company, that gap will cost you more than the tools ever save you.

post1.text:
The leaders most likely to derail your company's growth are the ones who stopped feeling like impostors.

Imposter syndrome gets treated like a problem to fix. It is not. It is a signal that you are operating at the edge of your competence, which is exactly where growth happens. For leaders steering companies past $50M, losing that internal friction is often the first sign of dangerous overconfidence.

A recent Campaign US piece made a compelling argument: instead of trying to eliminate imposter syndrome, high performers learn to channel it. That reframe matters enormously at scale.

Three things worth sitting with if you lead a $50M+ organization:

First, self-doubt that makes you ask better questions is an asset. Second, leaders who feel settled too early tend to stop stress-testing their assumptions. Third, the discomfort of rapid growth is not a warning to slow down. It is proof the work is real.

Your job is not to feel certain. Your job is to lead well under uncertainty.

So here is the question: When did you last let your self-doubt sharpen your thinking instead of silence it?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Campaign US flipped the conventional advice on imposter syndrome completely. The argument was not about overcoming it. It was about putting it to work.

That distinction matters a great deal for companies scaling past $50M.

At that stage, nearly every leader is operating in territory they have never navigated before. New markets, larger teams, higher stakes decisions. The leaders who perform best are not the ones who feel most confident. They are the ones who stay curious, stay accountable, and refuse to let discomfort become avoidance.

At Autobahn Consultants, we see this play out constantly with our clients. The growth ceiling is rarely a strategy problem. It is often a leadership psychology problem.

What does it mean to build a company past $50M in revenue and still wonder if you belong in the room?

Chapter 9 of Rock Your Business tackles that question directly. The chapter is titled "How Could You Be Successful and Not Have It?" and it was authored by Samantha Frost, Caleb Hawkins, and Rafa Loyo.

What makes their perspective worth your time is this: they are not writing about imposter syndrome as a personal weakness. They are writing about it as a leadership dynamic that shapes how entire organizations make decisions, take risks, and scale.

One insight they surface that most leaders are not prepared for: your team reads your self-doubt, and how you carry it determines whether it spreads as anxiety or models as humility.

That single shift in framing can change how you show up at the leadership level.

post1.text:
Most founders treat life planning like it's something they'll get to after the business is sorted. That's backwards.

Research consistently shows that leaders who fail to define what they actually want from their lives before hitting major financial milestones end up with serious regret. A recent Entrepreneur piece confirmed this hard truth: three out of four founders who sell their business feel that regret within just twelve months. The money arrives. The meaning doesn't.

For leaders scaling past $50M, here's what that means in practice:

1. Your business plan and your life plan need to be built in parallel, not in sequence. One informs the other.

2. Knowing your personal financial floor changes every strategic decision you make. It is not a soft concept. It is a hard number.

3. The energy you bring to your company at $50M is not sustainable at $200M without intentional design around how you work and recover.

The question is not whether you have a succession plan. The question is whether you have a life worth succeeding into.

What does your ideal day look like two years after the exit?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Entrepreneur reported that 75% of founders regret selling their business within a year of closing the deal. That number should stop every scaling CEO cold.

At Autobahn Consultants, we see this pattern well before the exit. Leaders who pour everything into growing from $50M to $200M and beyond often arrive at the finish line without ever asking what the finish line was actually for.

The fix is not more financial planning. It is earlier, more honest life planning. What do you want your time to look like? Your relationships? Your purpose? Those are not soft questions. They are strategic ones.

If you are building toward a major liquidity event, start designing the life on the other side now, not after the wire hits.

Read the full article here: https://news.google.

post3.text:
The data is clear: most founders do not regret building the business. They regret not knowing what they were building it for.

Chapter 10 of Rock Your Business, titled Coming Up for Air, tackles this directly. Authors Samantha Frost and Jonathan and Katherine Slain make a case that life planning is not a personal indulgence for scaling executives. It is a performance requirement.

One insight from that chapter that reframes everything: the leaders who sustain growth from $50M to $500M are not the ones who work harder. They are the ones who get deliberate about what sustains them outside the business before the business demands everything from them.

There is a framework in that chapter that connects your personal vision to your company's growth trajectory in a way that most leadership books never attempt.
